catalog_quote: Emihavani, like all Emakhuwa varieties, exhibits a contrast between H tone and the absence of a H tone (= toneless). H tones can only associate to moras. ... Emihavani, like all Emakhuwa dialects, has limited lexical tone. Nouns have a limited degree of unpredictability, particularly due to Emihavani’s extensive borrowing of Chichewa words ... Verb stems, on the other hand, do not have any lexical tonal contrasts. Pre-stem elements do have an unpredictable tone pattern, but the macrostem tone shape is entirely a function of the assignment of melodic H tones. ... Emihavani is one of the dialects that lacks this High Tone Doubling rule. ... In the case of Emihavani, word-final H tones are allowed. new_statements.rule_in_words: The only modern primary description treats Emihavani (Malawian Elomwe) as a Makhuwa-type restricted tone language: privative H vs toneless on moras, H placed by morphology (melodic H on macrostem mora 1, 2, stem mora 3, or final) plus limited nominal lexical H; no tone doubling; phrase-final H strongly suppressed. No statement anywhere about word stress, accent, or penultimate lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tonal: Chichewa loans give nouns some unpredictable H; yes-no questions exempt from phrase-final H suppression.)
new_statements.domain_note: Tone description; H realisation conditioned by phonological-phrase-final position. No word-level or phrase-level stress domain discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes Emihavani, the largest dialect of Malawian 'Elomwe' (speaker Alfred Lihelu; authors also collected Emunyamwelo, Ekokholani and a Chiradzulu variety, all 'highly similar'). This is Glottolog mala1256 Malawi Lomwe [lon] (alt. names Mihavane/Muhavani listed by OLAC for lon), not Mozambican Lomwe lomw1241 [ngl]; the authors treat all of these as dialects of Emakhuwa and find no linguistic basis for grouping Malawian with Mozambican Elomwe.

sources.locator: Sec. 2.2 'Tone', p. 5 (first sentence) and p. 6 (lexical tone; word-final H)
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent or penultimate lengthening. Sec. 2.2 'Tone' (pp. 5-6): Emihavani (largest 'Elomwe' dialect of Malawi) has a privative H vs toneless contrast on moras, no High Tone Doubling, word-final H allowed but radically suppressed phrase-finally, limited lexical tone in nouns and none in verb stems; rest of paper = melodic H assignment in verbs. Appendix p. 29: 'there is no literature known to us on the structure of Emihavani'.
